newsitem.title: USA: U.S. court says Chinese man can seek asylum.
newsitem.headline: U.S. court says Chinese man can seek asylum.

text.p: A Chinese technical expert who defected from a delegation he was leading to the United States in 1992 may seek asylum from the U.S. Attorney General, a federal appeals court has ruled.
A three-judge panel of the U.S. Third Circuit Court of Appeals made its ruling in a 2-1 decision dated Tuesday.

The court held that Chang Fenchu's 1992 defection was based on a fear that he would be politically persecuted for counteracting Chinese government orders that he inform on other delegation members he suspected would remain in the United States.
This fear made him eligible to apply to the attorney general for asylum as a refugee, the court held.
The decision overturned a finding by a federal immigration appeals board that Chang's defection lacked a political basis. The board ordered him in 1996 to leave the United States.

Said the appeals court, in reference to Chang, "He took a personal risk to defy the (Chinese) government because of the manner in which the government would punish other delegates. To characterise this action and Chang's motivation as anything other than political narrows the term 'political' beyond recognition."

It said Chang's status as chief engineer for a state-owned company, director of a state research institute and consultant to a government ministry, which gave him access to confidential information about state projects, left him particularly vulnerable to persecution.
In addition, the court noted that an FBI agent had met with Chang and warned him that he was "in danger" and had no choice but to seek asylum.

The incident stems from the visit of an eight-person technical delegation led by Chang to the United States in 1992. The team was to purchase technology for Chang's company from the U.S. firm Pangborn Corp.
According to a court summary, Chang developed suspicions that at least three members of the delegation were considering remaining in the United States.

As head of the delegation, Chang was required to report these suspicions to the Chinese embassy, but refused to, the appeals court found, out of concern that delegation members he had informed on would be mistreated even if they returned.

After another delegation member threatened to report Chang for not informing on the others, he became concerned for his own fate and discussed the issue with an employee of the American firm who had noticed his distress.

That employee then referred Chang to the FBI agent, although Chang was not aware of the agent's affiliation in the initial meeting. The agent accompanied Chang to an immigration service officer in Baltimore. Soon after, Chang applied for asylum, which was later rejected by the Immigration and Naturalisation Service.
